than October 2026 (see profiles of main Israeli political parties and their leaders in Appendix B). Netanyahu or the Knesset could call for elections to take place as early as September. In April
2026, Bennett and Lapid announced that they would contest this year's elections together in a new party known as Beyachad (Together). As of June, polls signal that Eisenkot's Yashar (Upright) party
could eclipse Beyachad as the top challenger to Netanyahu and Likud.64 Opposition to Netanyahu from figures who share some of Netanyahu's right-of-center political views increased after various
corruption allegations emerged against Netanyahu in the late 2010s\\u2014he was indicted in 2019 for fraud, breach of trust, and accepting a bribe, and his criminal trial remains
ongoing.65\\n...\\nNetanyahu's current government (see Table 1), which took office in late 2022, features two ultra-nationalist figures who openly support Israeli annexation of at least some West Bank

and construction in the West Bank, and he has taken corresponding actions aimed at further legitimizing Israeli civilian control in the West Bank at the expense of the Palestinian Authority.67 Ben
Gvir has used his control over Israel's police and other internal security to make appointments to key positions that seemingly diminish checks on extremist settlers in the West Bank, and increasingly

NBC News to Google\\n\\nAug. 7, 2026, 7:17 AM EDT / Source: Reuters\\n\\nBy Reuters\\n\\nIsrael\\u2019s far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich faces a fight for political survival in elections in
October after angering his fellow West Bank settlers by voting not to punish ultra-Orthodox Jews who refuse to serve in the military.\\n\\nThe political travails of Smotrich are a sign of how tricky
it will be for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to shepherd allies in his quarrelsome coalition through the Oct. 27 election, Israel\\u2019s first since the start of the Gaza war.\\n\\nA lifelong
settler in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, Smotrich, 46, leads the Religious Zionism party, which opposes a Palestinian state and argues that Jews\\u2019 claim to land between the Jordan River and
Mediterranean Sea arises from the Bible.\\n\\nSeveral Western countries have banned him from entering over accusations he supports violence by settlers against Palestinians in the West Bank, which he
and the Israeli government reject.\\n\\nThough less overtly pugnacious than the other main far-right cabinet member, Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, with whom he is often compared, Smotrich has
used his time in office to ramp up settlement building. He defends the cause with a caustic turn of phrase and is still lionised by many in the movement.\\n\\n\\u201cI think his achievements have been
off the charts,\\u201d said Chaim Silberstein, a settler in Beit El, where Smotrich grew up and where new apartment blocks reflect the expansion he has championed.\\n\\nBut some one-time backers have
been infuriated by his support last month for a law that would prevent the arrest of ultra-Orthodox Jews for avoiding the military draft.\\n\\n\\u201cI don\\u2019t have a political home today,\\u201d
said Sarel Halperin, 30, from the West Bank settlement of Alon Shvut, who voted for Religious Zionism in 2022. \\u201cIf we keep doing this for years we won\\u2019t have reservists and we won\\u2019t
have an army and we aren\\u2019t a country that can exist without an army.\\u201d\\n\\n## Calculated decision\\n\\nReligious Zionists such as Smotrich and his followers \\u2014 colloquially known as
\\u201cknitted kippahs\\u201d for the skullcaps worn by Orthodox Jewish men with modern dress \\u2014 believe Judaism and nationalism go hand in hand. That causes political friction with some ultra-
Orthodox communities in traditional dress, whose sons have typically eschewed military service for biblical study.\\n\\nParties representing both groups are part of Netanyahu\\u2019s coalition, which
has struggled to avert a split over the issue since a Supreme Court ruling in 2024 that an exemption to the draft for religious study was unlawful.\\n\\nSmotrich waves a national flag to supporters at
an Independence Day celebration in Sanur, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank in April.Hilel Ben Or / Middle East Images/AFP via Getty\\n\\nThe bill that passed in parliament last month would have
prevented arrests of ultra-Orthodox Jews who avoid the draft, but has also been blocked by the Supreme Court.\\n\\nSmotrich says the ultra-Orthodox should be obliged to serve, but that arresting them
would create division. He defended the position at a settler event last month, where attendees heckled him while shouting out numbers of dead soldiers.\\n\\n\\u201cArrests don\\u2019t bring ultra-
Orthodox to the army...they just make Jews fight one another in the streets,\\u201d he responded. \\u201cWe must enlist the ultra-Orthodox but it must be with a process and
consensus.\\u201d\\n\\nGayil Talshir, political science lecturer at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said Smotrich\\u2019s position represents a calculated decision to avoid a firm stance against
the exemption that would have forced him to quit the coalition.\\n\\n## \\u2018No longer represents values\\u2019\\n\\nRemaining in government allowed him to advance his goals and push settlement
expansion. But it has come at a cost in support from some who consider the issue fundamental.\\n\\nSmotrich \\u201cno longer represents the values of Religious Zionism\\u201d and has \\u201csold this
country to the ultra-Orthodox,\\u201d said Shvut Raanan, a 33-year-old lawyer who grew up in the West Bank and has campaigned to end the exemption from military service.\\n\\nHer husband has served
hundreds of days in the reserves since the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel that led to the Gaza war, and she said many households are crumbling under such strain.\\n\\nNBC News speaks with
Palestinian in West Bank whose home is surrounded by Israeli settlers\\n\\n06:02\\n\\nThe issue has not been as big a problem for Ben-Gvir, the other main far-right settler cabinet member, whose
voters are less motivated over the exemption, said Talshir.\\n\\nSmotrich\\u2019s party now holds seven seats in the 120-seat parliament, after running in 2022 on a combined list with Ben-Gvir\\u2019s
party that jointly won 14.\\n\\nOpinion polls lately indicate Religious Zionism would struggle to breach the minimum 3.5% of the vote needed to win any seats in October.\\n\\nStill, with every seat
likely to count in forming the next government, Talshir said she expected Netanyahu would try to arrange another party merger on the far right for Smotrich, to ensure his ally makes it

the US-led Board of Peace proposed a 15-point roadmap for Gaza, detailing a phased, conditional framework for disarmament and reconstruction in the war-torn coastal enclave.\\n...\\nThe plan mandates
that Hamas disarm in exchange for a full Israeli military withdrawal and the transition of governance to an independent Palestinian National Committee, supported by an international security
force.\\n...\\nThe Board of Peace, created by Trump in October with him serving as its lifetime chair, is led by the US government. United Nations Security Council (UNSC) Resolution 2803 designates it

he is on course to lose, said that Hamas must give up all of its weapons.\\n...\\n\\u201cWe are talking about real disarmament, not fictitious disarmament,\\u201d Netanyahu said.\\n...\\nAl

Updated Aug. 9, 2026, 9:53 AM EDT\\n\\nIsrael will not accept the 15-point plan for Gaza set out by President Donald Trump\\u2019s Board of Peace, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said
Sunday.\\n\\n\\u201cI want to clarify this: Israel rejects the 15-point document. I have heard people saying, \\u2018You didn\\u2019t say that.\\u2019 So here I am saying it again,\\u201d he told a
Cabinet meeting, referring to the peace plan set out by Trump last year. \\u201cThe IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed,\\u201d he added.\\n\\nTrump last month touted a
breakthrough in his Gaza peace plan, saying that Hamas has agreed to lay down arms.\\n\\nThe peace plan called for a phased withdrawal of Israel\\u2019s troops from Gaza alongside the disarmament of
Hamas, but Netanyahu said Israeli forces are not going anywhere until Hamas completely disarms first.\\n\\n\\u201cWhen I say Hamas must be disarmed, I mean heavy weapons, lighter weapons, all weapons.
We are talking about genuine disarmament, not a fictitious one,\\u201d Netanyahu said Sunday.\\n\\nHamas had last month said that it would disarm, but only after Israel withdraws completely and stops
all hostilities. The group also said that laying down its heavy weapons would come later in the process, conditional on the establishment of a Palestinian state.\\n\\nNetanyahu, meanwhile, reaffirmed
that \\u201cas long as I am prime minister, there will be no Palestinian state.\\u201d The leader is currently facing a domestic political battle for survival ahead of elections set for October, with
the status of the Gaza and Iran wars likely to prove pivotal.\\n\\nThe explicit rejection of the peace plan, frequently touted by Trump as a key foreign policy achievement, also comes after months of
growing tensions between the White House and Israel\\u2019s leadership over Iran. The White House did not immediately comment on the remarks.\\n\\nNetanyahu said of Washington: \\u201cWe are currently
discussing this issue with the Americans. They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand firm on these matters.\\u201d\\n\\nThe Israeli leader may
consider it worthwhile to \\u201center a new confrontation with President Trump,\\u201d said Ronni Shaked, a research fellow at the Harry S. Truman Institute at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, as
his own popularity wanes ahead of October\\u2019s election.\\n\\n\\u201cAfter three years, he is without any victory, and he just wants to show now to the people of Israel, before the election, that

\"highlights\": [\"Kushner and Netanyahu agree U.S. general should oversee Hamas \\u2018demilitarization,\\u2019 source says\\n...\\nKushner and Netanyahu meet over potential Gaza peace
plan\\n...\\nAug. 17, 2026, 6:24 AM EDT / Updated Aug. 18, 2026, 5:47 AM EDT\\n...\\nIsraeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Donald Trump\\u2019s son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner on
Monday agreed that the Gaza Strip\\u2019s \\u201cdemilitarization\\u201d should start with a Hamas weapons handover supervised by an American military general, according to a senior Israeli
official.\\n...\\nThe agreement came during an hourslong meeting, which followed rare talks between the leader of Hamas, Kushner and other members of Trump\\u2019s Board of Peace\\u2014 part of a
renewed push to revive a Gaza peace plan endorsed by Trump and Hamas but rejected by Israel.\\n...\\nNetanyahu and Kushner also agreed that no reconstruction of Gaza should begin before Hamas is
disarmed and that \\u201cnecessary measures\\u201d should be taken to \\u201caddress sanitation and environmental concerns,\\u201d the official added.\\n...\\nThe group \\u201cheld deep and
constructive discussions on the way forward,\\u201d a Board of Peace official told NBC News.\\n...\\nThey agreed the IDF would not redeploy from Gaza until Hamas is fully disarmed and agreed to
immediately establish joint working groups on the demilitarization of Gaza and the basic needs of the Palestinian enclave including clean water, the Board of Peace official said.\\n...\\nIn a
statement, Netanyahu\\u2019s office did not confirm the details given by the Israeli official but did confirm that the group had agreed to establish the two working groups.\\n...\\nBoth Israel and the
Board of Peace agree that the disarmament and demilitarization piece \\u201cshould be prompt and completed before any reconstruction happens in Gaza,\\u201d the prime minister\\u2019s office
said.\\n...\\nThe U.S. and Israel have shown rare public divisions over the road map for the future of the Palestinian enclave, as well as the Israeli government\\u2019s approach to a mounting crisis
in the occupied West Bank.\\n...\\nThe renewed diplomatic effort comes as Netanyahu faces growing domestic pressure ahead of Israeli elections in October, including from the far-right faction upon
which his fragile coalition government relies.\\n...\\nNetanyahu earlier this month rejected Trump\\u2019s 15-point plan, which would require Hamas\\u2019 disarmament and Israel\\u2019s withdrawal
from Gaza, with the Israeli leader vowing that there would be no military pullout until Hamas is \\u201cgenuinely disarmed.\\u201d\\n...\\nEarlier Monday, Hamas welcomed a joint statement from the
United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Jordan, Indonesia, Pakistan, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Egypt condemning Israel\\u2019s rejection of the road map.\\n...\\nHamas has said that it will disarm but that Israel
must end its strikes and begin withdrawing from Gaza. It has also previously said that laying down its heavy weapons, which would unfold later in the process, would be contingent on the international
recognition of a Palestinian state, a demand Israel\\u2019s current government rejects.\\n...\\nA Board of Peace official told NBC News over the weekend that the U.S. and Israel agreed on the
\\u201cend state\\u201d of talks, \\u201cwhich is a demilitarized Hamas.\\u201d\\n...\\n\\u201cWe will hear the concerns that have been raised and talk about next steps,\\u201d the official had said
of the meeting with Netanyahu. \\u201cWhat is critical is that we both agree on the desired outcome and are finding ways to accelerate progress.\\u201d\\n...\\nBut many in Israel do not want to

and other Palestinian terror groups violated the ceasefire 16 times between August 1 and 18, according to Israeli reports.\\n...\\nSince the Board of Peace announced its July 31 Hamas disarmament

publicly rejected that formula, saying Israel would not leave its current lines until Hamas was completely disarmed.\\n...\\nWashington responded by shifting from an all-at-once roadmap to a step-by-
step implementation strategy of Hamas compliance. On August 16, Jared Kushner and other US and Board of Peace officials met Hamas political leader Khalil al Hayya in Egypt. The group privately
reaffirmed its willingness to demilitarize and transfer governing authority, though its public statement did not explicitly repeat the disarmament pledge. Kushner then met Netanyahu for nearly four
hours on August 17. The emerging formula is that Hamas must first take a visible, verifiable step\\u2014such as surrendering weapons\\u2014before Israel makes concessions.\\n...\\nThe plan\\u2019s
disarmament mechanism was also partially fleshed out. Hamas weapons would be transferred through the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) for decommissioning and ultimately
destruction, with American-backed verification led by officers such as US Major General Jasper Jeffers. Israeli officials also discussed possible US military supervision. Netanyahu and Kushner further
agreed that major reconstruction would not begin before demilitarization. They established a working group on Hamas\\u2019s disarmament and another on sanitation and water.\\n...\\nMeanwhile, Israeli
strikes briefly fell under US pressure, then resumed as the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said Hamas operatives were rebuilding military capabilities, moving weapons, planning attacks, and crossing
ceasefire lines. Washington and Israel also agreed to create a deconfliction mechanism involving Egyptian mediators, but Israel retains the right to strike imminent threats. An unresolved question is

up 3-month Rafah operation in \", \"highlights\": [\"Netanyahu, Kushner Reach Gaza Roadmap Agreements As Hamas Disarmament Remains Key Condition - i24NEWS\\n...\\n# IDF will remain in Gaza until Hamas
is fully disarmed, Board of Peace official tells i24NEWS\\n...\\nIsrael and Board of Peace agree on Hamas disarmament, destruction of its weapons and tunnels, while two joint working groups will
oversee security and humanitarian efforts in Gaza\\n...\\nIsraeli Prime Minister Netanyahu and the Board of Peace have agreed that there will be no redeployment of Israeli forces from Gaza until Hamas
is fully disarmed and the territory is completely demilitarized, a Board of Peace official told i24NEWS.\\n...\\nThe understanding was reached during more than three hours of talks Monday between
Netanyahu, US President Trump\\u2019s envoy Jared Kushner and senior Israeli, American and Board of Peace officials, as the parties moved toward implementing the next stage of Trump\\u2019s 20-point
Gaza peace plan.\\n...\\nAccording to the Board of Peace official, Hamas has committed to \\u201cfully disarm\\u201d and immediately halt all military activity in Gaza, including rearmament and the
construction of tunnels.\\n...\\nThe agreement stipulates that all weapons, light and heavy, must be collected and permanently decommissioned, while Gaza\\u2019s tunnel network must also be
dismantled.\\n...\\nIsrael, meanwhile, will retain what the Board of Peace described as its \\u201cfull right of self-defense.\\u201d If Hamas resumes terrorist activity, violence or attempts to
rearm, Israel will retain the right to take action, the official said.\\n...\\nThe agreement also means there will be no IDF redeployment from Gaza until Hamas has been fully disarmed and the
territory demilitarized. Israeli forces will also not withdraw from the so-called Yellow Line during this stage of the process.\\n...\\nThe talks also produced an understanding that reconstruction and
broader rehabilitation efforts in Gaza will not move forward until Hamas\\u2019 disarmament has been completed.\\n...\\nAccording to sources familiar with the discussions, Hamas must begin handing
over its weapons if it wants to demonstrate that the disarmament process is genuine and viable. The weapons surrendered by Hamas will not be transferred to a future Palestinian governing body.
Instead, they will be destroyed.\\n...\\nDuring the initial phase, Hamas is expected to hand the weapons directly to an American force, with their destruction carried out under the responsibility and
supervision of US General Jasper Jeffers.\\n...\\nThe Board of Peace said the talks also addressed Israel\\u2019s previous commitments under the agreement that helped secure the release of all
hostages, including the living hostages and, tragically, the remains of those who were killed.\\n...\\nTo coordinate the next phase, Israel and the Board of Peace agreed to establish two joint working
groups immediately. One will focus on security and the complete demilitarization of Gaza, while the second will address basic humanitarian needs, including sanitation, clean water and public
health.\\n...\\nSanitation has emerged as an immediate priority amid concerns over deteriorating conditions in Gaza and the risk of disease outbreaks.\\n...\\nThe discussions brought together senior
Israeli, American and Board of Peace officials. Israeli participants included Shin Bet chief David Zini, the head of the National Security Council and Netanyahu\\u2019s military secretary. The Board
of Peace delegation included senior officials Nikolay Mladenov and Tony Blair, while US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee and American military officers also took part.\\n...\\nIn an interview with
Channel 12, Mladenov warned that dismantling Hamas\\u2019 extensive tunnel network could take as long as 10 years, underscoring the scale of the demilitarization challenge facing the
parties.\\n...\\nThe Board of Peace official said the sides share a broader objective, backed by Trump: creating a \\u201cfully demilitarized and deradicalized Gaza\\u201d that no longer poses a
threat to Israel and where Palestinians can pursue \\u201cprosperity and dignity peacefully.\\u201d\\n...\\nThe agreements mark a move toward the implementation phase of the Gaza roadmap, with
Hamas\\u2019 complete disarmament emerging as the central condition for any further Israeli redeployment and reconstruction of the Strip.\"], \"published_date\": \"2026-08-17T00:00:00.000\",

\"highlights\": [\"Kushner: Gaza demilitarization could begin within 30 days - Israel & Jewish News - JNS\\n...\\n# Kushner: Gaza demilitarization could begin within 30 days\\n...\\n## \\u201cAnd

Kushner said on Monday that progress toward Gaza\\u2019s demilitarization could begin within 30 days, following a nearly four-hour meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin
Netanyahu.\\n...\\nKushner told Fox News that Washington would not support rebuilding Gaza before demilitarization, adding that the administration had addressed Israeli concerns about the Board of
Peace roadmap and clarified that Israel\\u2019s right to act against imminent threats would not be restricted.\\n...\\n\\u201cWe could be seeing progress in as little 30 days, hopefully on starting to
take some of the weapons out, and hopefully filling in some of the tunnels as well in the next 60 to 90 days,\\u201d Kushner said, adding that progress would require cooperation from both
sides.\\n...\\nNetanyahu and representatives of the Board of Peace, the U.S.-backed transitional international body overseeing postwar Gaza and chaired by U.S. President Donald Trump, held \\u201cdeep
and constructive\\u201d discussions on Monday, according to the Prime Minister\\u2019s Office in Jerusalem.\\n...\\nThe sides agreed to establish two working groups, including one focused on the
disarmament and demilitarization of Gaza. It was also agreed that the process should be completed promptly before any reconstruction begins in the Strip, according to the PMO
statement.\\n...\\nIsraeli President Isaac Herzog also met on Monday with Kushner and Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace\\u2019s High Representative for Gaza, to discuss the next steps in
implementing the roadmap.\\n...\\nFollowing the meeting, Herzog said he was \\u201cimpressed that Israel\\u2019s security interests are an important and central element\\u201d of the proposal. He also
praised the Board of Peace\\u2019s efforts to promote a \\u201cbrighter and more secure future\\u201d for Israelis, Palestinians and the broader region.\\n...\\nThe meetings came after a Hamas
delegation began talks in Egypt on Sunday to probe alternative ways of advancing the 15-point roadmap, a Hamas official told AFP.\\n...\\nThe source was quoted as saying that talks would cover
\\u201cthe latest developments in the negotiations and the efforts being made to compel Israel to abide by the agreement,\\u201d apparently referring to previous Hamas statements that it would start
handing its arms to a technocratic Palestinian body only after the Israel Defense Forces withdraw from the Gaza Strip.\\n...\\nThe delegation, led by Hamas chief Khalil al-Hayya, started its meetings
with Egyptian intelligence chief Hassan Rashad in the city of El-Alamein, situated on the Mediterranean coast northwest of Cairo, the official said.\\n...\\nLeaders of the terrorist group also
reportedly met with Kushner.\\n...\\nIsraeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich on Tuesday praised Netanyahu for insisting on the \\u201cgenuine dismantling and demilitarization\\u201d of Hamas and
Gaza, but said defeating the terrorist group would require full Israeli control of the Strip, renewed Israeli settlement and the pursuit of Hamas terrorists worldwide.\\n...\\nSmotrich said that goal
was incompatible with negotiations with Hamas leaders, \\u201cwho should not be alive at all,\\u201d calling that the \\u201croot of the mistake\\u201d in the Trump-backed 15-point plan and saying
Jerusalem must make its position clear to the U.S. administration.\\n...\\nOn Tuesday, U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee said that there was no disagreement between Israel and the United States
over disarming Hamas and ensure the terrorist group has no future in the Gaza Strip.\\n...\\nHuckabee, who attended meetings on Monday with Netanyahu, described the talks as \\u201cintense and

\"highlights\": [\"Hamas meets Jared Kushner, Board of Peace delegation for Gaza talks in Cairo | The Jerusalem Post\\n...\\n# Kushner, Blair, BoP head Mladenov meet Hamas delegation in Cairo over
Gaza roadmap, sources say\\n...\\n## Hamas, US, and Board of Peace delegations discuss disarmament, decommissioning of terror infrastructure \\u2022 Talks also included IDF withdrawal and Gaza's
reconstruction, source tells 'Post'\\n...\\nUS envoy Jared Kushner, former British prime minister Tony Blair, and Gazan Board of Peace (BoP) Director-General Nikolay Mladenov met with a Hamas
delegation in Cairo on Sunday to discuss the implementation of the BoP\\u2019s 15-point roadmap for the Gaza Strip, a source familiar with the matter told The Jerusalem Post.\\n...\\nThe source said
that the objective of the meeting was to translate the steps outlined in Mladenov\\u2019s roadmap into concrete, verifiable actions aimed at maintaining the ceasefire between Hamas and Israel and
removing Hamas from power in Gaza.\\n...\\nThe meeting also covered the transfer of all governing responsibilities in the Strip to the technocratic National Committee for the Administration of Gaza
(NCAG), as well as the deployment of the International Stabilization Force (ISF).\\n...\\nAccording to the source, the US and Hamas delegations also discussed the decommissioning of Hamas weapons and
terror infrastructure, IDF withdrawal, and reconstruction and humanitarian relief efforts in Gaza.\\n...\\nThe source told the Post that \\u201cthere can be no ambiguity: Hamas must relinquish

# Gaza Second-Phase Negotiations: Schedule & Status, August–September 2026

## Bottom line up front

**Israel has already formally rejected the 15-point plan — twice — and as of today (Aug 19, 2026) has not reversed that.** On Aug 9, Netanyahu told a televised cabinet meeting: *"I wish to be precise here: Israel does not accept the 15-point document."* At the Aug 17 Kushner meeting he reaffirmed it. Critically, **the US response has been to route around the need for Israeli formal acceptance** rather than to force it — substituting bilateral "understandings" and joint working groups for endorsement of the document itself.

**No summit, Board of Peace plenary, signing ceremony, or deadline is scheduled in the Aug 19 – Sept 10 window.** I found no announced diplomatic event at which formal acceptance would naturally occur.

---

## 1. The document and its acceptance mechanism

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Name | "Roadmap for Completing the Implementation of President Trump's Comprehensive Peace Plan in Gaza" |
| Dated | July 30, 2026 (Trump announcement); full text published July 31 |
| Author | Board of Peace (Trump = chair for life; Mladenov = High Representative for Gaza) |
| Legal frame | Trump 20-point plan + UNSC Resolution 2803 (2025) |
| Hamas status | **Accepted** (July 30–31), reaffirmed in Cairo Aug 16 |
| Israel status | **Formally rejected** Aug 9; not reversed |

**There is no defined signing ceremony or ratification vote for the roadmap.** The text refers only to "all parties approve the Roadmap" as the trigger event. Two clocks start on approval:
- Art. 2: Phase 2 timetable + implementation mechanisms prepared **within 14 days** (extendable by the International Verification Committee)
- Art. 8: weapons-decommissioning timetable, same 14 days

The BBC reported seeing an annex requiring **Israeli forces to withdraw to the Yellow Line "within 24 hours of the Israeli government's approval of the plan."** This is precisely the consequence Netanyahu is avoiding — it makes formal acceptance an immediately operative act, not a symbolic one.

---

## 2. Timeline of Israel's position

- **July 26** — Security Cabinet approves ISF entry in principle, ISF immunity, and a Board of Peace pilot in Rafah. *Smotrich voted for; Ben Gvir voted against.*
- **Aug 3** — Israel conveys formal objections to Washington. IDF halts airstrikes.
- **Aug 4** — Netanyahu: *"They sent us a draft. We did not agree to it. It was not our draft. We sent back our comments."*
- **Aug 9** — Explicit public rejection at cabinet. "Heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry… genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament." Adds: *"As long as I am Prime Minister, a Palestinian state will not be established."* **Smotrich publicly claims credit**: "I congratulate the Prime Minister for responding to our demand."
- **Aug 16** — Kushner, Mladenov, Blair meet Hamas delegation (Khalil al-Hayya) in Egypt (Cairo/El-Alamein), >2 hrs — unprecedented direct high-level US–Hamas engagement. Kushner also meets Sisi. Eight Arab/Muslim states (Saudi, UAE, Egypt, Qatar, Jordan, Indonesia, Pakistan, Türkiye) issue a joint statement condemning Israel's rejection.
- **Aug 17** — Kushner + Mladenov + Blair + Huckabee meet Netanyahu in Jerusalem, ~4 hours. Israeli side included Shin Bet chief Zini and MI chief Binder.
- **Aug 18–19** — Israeli strikes resume (Nukhba commanders, PIJ commander). Smotrich attacks the plan's premise. Huckabee denies any rift as "fake news."

### What the Aug 17 meeting actually produced

**Agreed:** two joint working groups (disarmament/demilitarization; sanitation/water/public health); US Maj. Gen. Jasper Jeffers (ISF commander) to supervise weapons handover and destruction; a deconfliction mechanism; no reconstruction before full disarmament.

**Not agreed:** Israeli acceptance of the roadmap. AP: *"no concrete commitment by Israel."* Guardian: *"no breakthrough."* Israeli officials explicitly denied agreeing to halt targeted killings or reduce troop levels.

The framing gap is telling. A Board of Peace official: *"The Israelis are going to give this a chance. Now it's up to Hamas."* Per CNN, **Netanyahu told Kushner and Mladenov that progress on the 15-point framework was politically "problematic" ahead of the October 27 election.**

Note the substantive inversion: the roadmap's core logic was *synchronization* — phased disarmament matched to phased withdrawal. The Aug 17 understandings invert it to **disarmament first, withdrawal later**, which is Israel's position, not the document's. Washington moved toward Israel; Israel did not move toward the document.

---

## 3. Scheduled events before September 10, 2026

**I found none that would serve as an acceptance venue.**

| Candidate | Status |
|---|---|
| Board of Peace announcements page | Last entry **July 30, 2026**. No forward calendar. |
| Board of Peace plenary/summit | None announced. (Inaugural meeting was Feb 19, 2026.) |
| Egypt/Cairo leaders' summit | None announced for this window |
| **UNGA 81 opening — Sept 8** | Procedural session only. **General debate is Sept 22–28 — after the deadline.** |
| Israeli cabinet meetings | Weekly Sundays: **Aug 23, Aug 30, Sept 6** — the only natural venues for a formal Israeli position change |
| Two new working groups | **No announced start date, composition, or timeline.** A senior Israeli official told Times of Israel they could not provide details. |

**Kushner's informal markers (Fox News, Aug 17):** weapons removal progress "in as little as 30 days" (≈ **Sept 16 — past the deadline**); tunnel filling in "60 to 90 days" (mid-Oct to mid-Nov). His framing: *"Either Hamas disarms willingly over the next 60 to 90 days, or Israel will have a lot more support from the US and others to go and finish the job."*

No ultimatum or deadline has been issued to **Israel**. The only ultimatum language in the record is directed at **Hamas**.

---

## 4. Israeli domestic politics — the binding constraint

- **Election: October 27, 2026.** Knesset dissolved July 17 — first full four-year term since 1988.
- **Israel has operated as a caretaker government since July 17**, with (per Xinhua) *"limited authority to advance major policy initiatives except for broadly supported legislation, routine regulatory matters and measures required for security needs."* Accepting the roadmap — which triggers withdrawal within 24 hours — is the archetype of a major policy initiative.
- **Polling (Channel 12):** Eizenkot's Yashar 23 · Likud 22 · Bennett–Lapid "Together" 16. Anti-Netanyahu bloc 59, pro-Netanyahu bloc 51, Arab parties 10 — **neither bloc reaches 61.**
- **Coalition pressure:** Smotrich's Religious Zionism is polling below the 3.25% threshold and he has ruled out re-merging with Ben Gvir — he needs maximal hardline differentiation. Ben Gvir was the sole cabinet vote against ISF deployment and has made dismissing the Attorney General a condition of joining any future coalition.
- Netanyahu has not delivered the "absolute victory" he promised; Israel controls **>60% of Gaza**, up from 53% at the October 2025 Yellow Line.

**Analyst consensus is unusually tight:**
- Aaron David Miller: *"It's hard to believe that you're going to see any serious movement before you have another Israeli government."*
- Shira Efron (RAND): *"Politically, in Israel, and especially before elections, it's borderline impossible for the Israeli government to accept [the plan]."*
- Yossi Kuperwasser: *"No movement prior to [the] end of October."*
- Alon Pinkas: the rejection *"should be viewed entirely in the context of the upcoming Israeli election on October 27."*
- Julie Norman (Chatham House): even a *new* government would be "hard-pressed to suddenly make major concessions."

---

## 5. US posture — why pressure is unlikely to force acceptance

The White House is **not treating the rejection as a crisis.** A senior US official to Axios (Barak Ravid): *"We understand Bibi's political needs. We have no problem with it as long as he continues to do what we ask — especially regarding restraining attacks in Gaza."* Trump was uncharacteristically silent on Truth Social after Aug 9.

Trump on Fox, Aug 17: *"We have our own relationship with Hamas. They are giving up their guns."*

Al-Monitor reports the understandings were driven by "political exigencies — Israel's October elections and the US midterm elections." Signals of friction exist (Netanyahu's July 28 White House visit: side door, no red carpet, no press conference) but have not translated into leverage.

---

## 6. The strongest counter-signal

**Israel is substantially complying while publicly refusing.** Al-Monitor (Aug 11), citing a top Israeli diplomatic source: Israel authorized ISF entry July 26, suspended targeting of Hamas militants under US pressure, and halted airstrikes Aug 3–~Aug 11. The Board of Peace publicly praised Israel for adhering to the deal — **directly contradicting Netanyahu's own statement.** BBC's assessment: the rejection is *"unlikely to be the final word."*

But this cuts both ways for the forecast question. De facto compliance **reduces** the pressure for de jure acceptance: Netanyahu gets the substance the US wants while keeping the rejection his base requires. As Al Jazeera's analysts put it, this is a *"yes, but"* policy — "selective implementation" without the political cost of endorsement.

---

## 7. Market and quantitative signals

- **Manifold, "Will Hamas actually disarm in 2026?"** — **6.4%** (volume ~4,328 mana)
- **Noah Intelligence (Aug 3, *pre*-rejection):** 31% that the IVC certifies a first matched milestone by Sept 30, 2026; 46% that machinery is partially built but no certified milestone. Its stated downside trigger — "the 14-day mechanism deadline passes without a timetable" — **has since occurred.**
- No Polymarket or Kalshi market found on Israeli acceptance of the 15-point plan.

---

## 8. What would have to happen for acceptance by Sept 10

A concrete path exists but requires a chain of low-probability steps in ~3 weeks: Hamas begins a visible, verifiable weapons handover to Jeffers → the working groups produce a sequencing formula Israel can present as *its* terms rather than the roadmap's → Netanyahu convenes the security cabinet (Aug 23, Aug 30, or Sept 6) → he absorbs Smotrich/Ben Gvir defection risk ~7 weeks before the election → and the acceptance is framed as endorsing the document rather than a rebranded Israeli variant.

The most likely *partial* outcome, given the Aug 17 pattern, is further incremental understandings that stop short of the formal act — which would leave the question resolving NO even amid visible diplomatic progress. A significant resolution ambiguity: if Israel accepts a **modified** sequencing framework, whether that counts as accepting "the 15-point plan" depends on the question's precise wording.

## Summary

The research is complete and submitted. The decisive findings for the forecast:

**Israel has already formally rejected the plan and has not reversed it.** Netanyahu's Aug 9 statement was unusually explicit and deliberately repeated ("I have heard people saying: 'You didn't say it.' So here I am saying it again"). He reaffirmed the position at the Aug 17 Kushner meeting.

**Three structural facts work against acceptance by Sept 10:**

1. **No venue exists.** No Board of Peace plenary, summit, or signing event is scheduled in the window. UNGA's high-level week falls *after* the deadline (Sept 22–28; only the procedural opening is Sept 8). The only possible venues are the routine Sunday cabinet meetings of Aug 23, Aug 30, and Sept 6.

2. **Acceptance is immediately operative, not symbolic.** The annex BBC reviewed requires IDF withdrawal to the Yellow Line within 24 hours of Israeli government approval — which is exactly what Netanyahu is refusing, seven weeks before an election he is polling to lose.

3. **The US has stopped asking.** The most important dynamic is that Washington reshaped the process around Israel's refusal rather than confronting it — substituting working groups and a US-general verification mechanism, and flipping the roadmap's synchronized sequencing to Israel's disarmament-first ordering. A senior US official: "We understand Bibi's political needs. We have no problem with it as long as he continues to do what we ask."

**The main counter-consideration** is that Israel is substantively complying while publicly refusing — the Board of Peace has praised Israeli adherence, contradicting Netanyahu. But this arguably *lowers* the probability of formal acceptance: the current arrangement gives both sides what they need without it.

One flag for the forecaster: the roadmap defines no signing ceremony or ratification vote for itself, so "formal acceptance" has no canonical form. If Israel endorses a rebranded sequencing framework derived from the Aug 17 understandings, whether that resolves YES depends on the question's exact wording — worth checking against the resolution criteria.

results and insisting that the party list chosen by members would achieve a \\u201cbig victory\\u201d in the October 27 election.\\n...\\nNetanyahu appeared to have legitimate reason to celebrate,
with several hardliners whom he reportedly feared would harm the party\\u2019s popularity in the general election successfully shunted toward the back of the Likud electoral slate.\\n...\\nWith polls
consistently showing the Likud party likely to win fewer than 25 Knesset seats, only those who finished in the top 17 of Monday\\u2019s primary are seen as having a realistic shot of making it back to
the Knesset. The other eight spots are controlled by Netanyahu himself, whose position as party leader was not part of the primary vote.\\n...\\nAlmost certainly out of a job come October are
hardliners like MK Hanoch Milwidsky, MK Nissim Vaturi and Social Equality Minister May Golan, who declared Tuesday that she was \\u201ctoo right-wing\\u201d for Netanyahu.\\n...\\nFor Netanyahu,
facing the very real prospect of losing office, holding onto power may hinge on moderating the Likud slate to the point that the party becomes palatable again to voters who have fled over its turn to
the hard right in the last election. After successfully expanding his direct control over about a third of the top seats, Monday\\u2019s primary marked the latest test of his ability to shape the
Likud roster into something he can sell to potential supporters, one he seems to have passed with flying colors, though the real trial won\\u2019t take place until October 27.\\n...\\nIn the last
election, Likud won 32 seats, a number consistent with its showing in elections over the previous decade. Today, polls put it at around 23 seats, neck-and-neck with former IDF chief of staff Gadi
Eisenkot\\u2019s centrist Yashar party and almost certainly unable to scrape together another governing coalition.\\n...\\nMany of Likud\\u2019s former voters have moved toward more moderate right-
wing or even centrist parties that will likely bolster Eisenkot or Beyachad head Naftali Bennett\\u2019s bid to cobble together a government and oust Netanyahu from power.\\n...\\nHe cited a
poll\\n...\\nin favor of a national unity government between the right and center\\n...\\nprospect supported by\\n...\\n3.9\\n...\\nWhile bringing in more moderate candidates and pushing
down\\n...\\nless palatable to the average voter won\\u2019t change the widespread view of the party and its leadership as responsible for the failures of October 7 or erase voters\\u2019 memory of
its recent push to exempt Haredim from military service, it could help Likud with voters\\n...\\nremain on the fence, an important achievement in and of itself.\\n...\\nIf left up to primary voters
alone, Likud\\u2019s list would likely continue to pull toward the right.\\n...\\nA recent poll by\\n...\\nof 1,000\\n...\\nvoters unconnected to the internal wheeling and dealing that often plays a
major part in how members cast ballots found that firebrand MK Tally Gotliv and Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee chairman Boaz Bismuth, another member of the party\\u2019s far-right
flank, would be among the top three vote-getters.\\n...\\nInstead, the pair finished in 12th and 15th place respectively, with Netanyahu\\u2019s control of reserved slots likely pushing them all the
way down to slots 19 and 23. (Gotliv has alleged fraud, claiming that her name had been left off ballots at some polling stations.)\\n...\\nAt the same time as he pushed some unpalatable candidates
out, Netanyahu also threw a bone to the more hardline elements of the electorate by endorsing former Otzma Yehudit MK Almog Cohen, who came in at number 8 in the primary vote.\\n...\\n\\u201cThis was
an attempt to hold back Likud voters who defected to [Otzma Yehudit chairman and National Security Minister Itamar] Ben Gvir, which many did during these past few years, because Ben Gvir keeps on
giving the impression, and maybe rightfully so, that [Netanyahu] is holding him back from being even more nationalistic and security-driven,\\u201d Nir stated.\\n...\\nNetanyahu won control of the
reserved seats last month, when the Likud Central Committee agreed to greatly expand his control over the party\\u2019s Knesset slate.\\n...\\nHis push to secure the reserved spots was reportedly
based on concerns that the primary would elevate candidates who are highly popular among the Likud base, but whom internal party polling suggests are less appealing to moderate right-wing and swing
voters.\\n...\\nFive of those slots have already been handed out to Foreign Minister Gideon Sa\\u2019ar, Defense Minister Israel Katz, Likud Central Committee chair Haim Katz and political newcomer
Oren Dobronsky, with three more in the top 15 yet to be named, along with two others in spots\\n...\\n26 and 29.\\n...\\nAccording to Nir, Netanyahu can now use those spots to complete his crafting of
what he perceives as the slate most likely to raise Likud\\u2019s haul in the general election.\\n...\\nIt gives Netanyahu \\u201cthe opportunity to bring some more moderate people and some fresh
faces from the outside that will actually try to appeal to the larger voter audience rather than the party members,\\u201d he said.\"], \"published_date\": \"2026-08-18T17:17:08.000\", \"score\":

contro\", \"highlights\": [\"No one has managed the balancing act longer than Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel\\u2019s longest-serving leader. But with the Iran war at a stalemate, and U.S.
President Donald Trump looking to advance peace efforts elsewhere, Netanyahu\\u2019s task is getting harder less than three months away from Israeli elections.\\n...\\nOn Sunday, Netanyahu rejected
Trump\\u2019s latest plan to advance the stalled ceasefire in Gaza, saying Israel will not withdraw from any of the roughly 60% of the territory it controls until Hamas has been completely disarmed
\\u2014 something the militant group controlling the other 40% has long resisted.\\n...\\nNetanyahu risks angering Trump, who he has repeatedly said is the greatest friend Israel has ever had in the

Likud is paying the price\\n\\nAuthor: Ben-Dror Yemini\\nPublished: 2026-08-18T03:25:27.293184+00:00\\nSource: ynetnews.com (ynetnews.com)\\nLanguage: en\\n\\n## Story\\n\\nNetanyahu needed the far
right to survive. Now Likud is paying the price\\n\\n[Updates](https://www.ynetnews.com/category/3089) [Red Mail](https://www.ynetnews.com/category/43972)\\n\\n[![](https://ynet-
pic1.yit.co.il/static/Cnt/Images/Weather/1220.png)](https://www.ynetnews.com/weather/tel-aviv-yafo)\\n\\n\", \"highlights\": [\"## Opinion: Likud once prided itself on keeping Kahanist extremists
outside the political mainstream; Netanyahu\\u2019s fight for survival erased that boundary, and the primaries now suggest the far right he legitimized may be reshaping the party from
within\\n...\\nBenjamin Netanyahu spent years tearing that barrier down. Not necessarily because he embraced every element of that ideology himself, but because his political survival increasingly
depended on assembling every possible faction of the Israeli right into a governing majority. Each election, each coalition crisis and each threat to his rule made the far right more useful. And each
time Netanyahu helped bring those forces closer to the political mainstream, they became a little more legitimate.\\n...\\nThat process has now reached the point where Netanyahu appears increasingly
concerned not only about the power of Itamar Ben-Gvir outside Likud, but about the influence of Ben-Gvir-style politics inside his own party. Reports ahead of the Likud primaries suggested concern in
Netanyahu\\u2019s camp that hard-line lawmakers such as Tally Gotliv and May Golan could eventually take their Knesset seats and defect to Ben-Gvir\\u2019s Otzma Yehudit after the election. But the
more revealing question is why they would need to defect at all. When the ideological distance between the two parties keeps shrinking, the distinction between them becomes increasingly difficult to
see.\\n...\\nIf only it were possible to blame the primaries. It is true that recent weeks produced a competition among candidates over who could take a harsher line against the attorney general, the
Supreme Court and anyone branded part of the \\u201cdeep state.\\u201d There was barely a word about the real issues confronting Israel: Iran, Hezbollah and Hamas, despite a government failure of
historic proportions. So what remains? Not merely pointing a finger at supposed enemies within, but waving a fist and promising that after the election they will settle scores, dismantle institutions
and perhaps even put their imagined enemies on trial.\\n...\\nThe deeper problem is that Likud\\u2019s radical wing no longer looks like an insurgency challenging the party from the margins. It
increasingly shapes the party\\u2019s tone. Figures such as Gotliv and Golan represent a political language and worldview that once would have stood far outside Likud\\u2019s accepted boundaries.
Golan has said that \\u201cthere are no ideological gaps between Otzma Yehudit and Likud.\\u201d Gotliv has repeatedly praised Ben-Gvir, who has openly invited her to join his party. Likud lawmaker
Nissim Vaturi has said that \\u201cKahane was right about many things\\u201d and that today he would receive the Israel Prize. These are not simply provocative remarks. They show how far the
ideological border has moved.\\n...\\nIn 2022, Netanyahu still understood that Ben-Gvir carried a political stigma. He refused to be photographed with him. Yet that did not stop Netanyahu from helping
bring Ben-Gvir\\u2019s political camp into the mainstream. He pushed alliances on the far right because he needed every possible vote to secure a governing majority. The calculation worked. But
political alliances change more than parliamentary arithmetic. They confer legitimacy. Once politicians who had been treated as beyond the democratic mainstream become coalition partners, ministers
and regular fixtures of government, their ideas stop appearing exceptional. They become part of the political conversation. Eventually, they become part of the governing party itself.\\n...\\nthat he
would prefer a more disciplined and less incendiary party list. If they win despite him, they may feel even less constrained by him. That is why these primaries matter. They are not simply an internal
contest over positions on a slate. They are a\\n...\\nThere was always a political logic behind Netanyahu\\u2019s strategy. The Israeli right is fragmented, and Netanyahu understood that elections
could be lost if votes on his side were wasted on parties that failed to enter the Knesset. Bringing small right-wing factions together was electorally rational. Without them, he risked losing power.
But that strategy came with a price. The forces Netanyahu helped normalize now have their own leaders, their own constituencies and increasingly their own representatives inside Likud.\\n...\\nAnd
that matters because Likud voters are not synonymous with the radical right. Many are traditional nationalists, security hawks and conservatives who see themselves as heirs to the movement of Begin
and David Levy. They are right-wing. They are not Kahanists. Yet Netanyahu\\u2019s endless battle for political survival has steadily weakened the distinction between those two traditions.\\n...\\nHe
needed the far right, so he legitimized it. He needed its voters, so he helped bring its leaders into the political mainstream. He needed coalition partners, so positions once considered beyond the
boundaries of Likud became negotiable. Now, with another election approaching and the primaries revealing how powerful the party\\u2019s radical wing has become, Netanyahu may be discovering that this
process cannot simply be reversed when it becomes inconvenient.\\n...\\nThe danger for Netanyahu is no longer merely that Likud politicians might defect to Ben-Gvir. It is that Ben-Gvir\\u2019s
politics have already moved into Likud.\"], \"published_date\": \"2026-08-18T03:25:27.000\", \"score\": null}, {\"title\": \"Pleasing no one: Netanyahu puts election first with Gaza decision - AL-
MONITOR: The Middle East\\u02bcs leading independent news source since 2012\", \"url\": \"https://www.al-monitor.com/originals/2026/08/pleasing-no-one-netanyahu-puts-election-first-gaza-decision\",
\"snippet\": \"Pleasing no one: Netanyahu puts election first with Gaza decision - AL-MONITOR: The Middle East\\u02bcs leading independent news source since 2012\\n\\n# Pleasing no one: Netanyahu puts
election first with Gaza decision\\n\\nShaun TANDON\\n\\nAug 10, 2026\\n\\nIsrael's far-right national security minister Itamar Ben Gvir (right) speaks to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in
parliament on July 16, 2026 \\u2014 ilia YEFIMOVICH\\n\\nFaced with a divisive US-led Gaza plan just before elections that could end his career, Israeli P\", \"highlights\": [\"Pleasing no one:
Netanyahu puts election first with Gaza decision - AL-MONITOR: The Middle East\\u02bcs leading independent news source since 2\\n...\\nFaced with a divisive US-led Gaza plan just before elections that
could end his career, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had to choose between pleasing his ally Donald Trump or his right-wing base.\\n...\\nIn rejecting the plan, he may not please
anyone.\\n...\\nThe decision is a tactical and PR victory for Hamas, analysts say, with the Islamist movement publicly backing the deal under which it would disarm, without taking any steps yet to do
so.\\n...\\nNetanyahu, who has built his decades-long career on hawkish security positions, had voiced concerns but softly after the US president on July 30 hailed what he called the historic
milestone on ending the Gaza war.\\n...\\nHe finally rejected the plan Sunday during a cabinet meeting after pushback from the far-right, which strongly opposes the 15-point deal that would see Israel
eventually withdraw troops from much of Gaza.\\n...\\nNetanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, is by nature \\\"a procrastinator\\\" and is struggling to secure the trust of the hard-right
ahead of the October 27 vote, said Yossi Mekelberg, an expert on Israeli politics at London-based think tank Chatham House.\\n...\\nNetanyahu's calculation is to dissuade votes for the opposition by
creating the impression that he is \\\"still the only bastion of power that will stop Hamas\\\", Mekelberg said.\\n...\\n\\\"Netanyahu knows that falling out with Trump doesn't serve him or Israel. On
the other hand, he knows the minute that he agrees to the 15 points, he would be attacked not only by the right wing but that some opposition parties will attack him, too,\\\" he
said.\\n...\\n\\\"He's trying to appease everyone. At the end of the day, he will be appeasing no one.\\\"\\n...\\nIsrael will be voting for the first time since the trauma of Hamas's October 7, 2023
attack, the deadliest ever against Israel, which retaliated with an overwhelming offensive in Gaza.\\n...\\nDespite Netanyahu's public rejection of Trump's plan, Israel in practice appears to be
complying with a key part of it. Israel has stopped air strikes since August 3, although Gaza authorities report periodic Israeli gunfire.\\n...\\n\\\"These strikes could be resumed and even
intensified at any time. It is one of the cards Israel can manoeuvre with,\\\" said Ehud Eilam, a former analyst at Israel's defence ministry.\\n...\\nHe noted that Israel had not succeeded in its
goal of completely destroying Hamas after October\\n...\\n\\\"Therefore, Israel at least seeks to disarm Hamas, which is also a very difficult task,\\\" Eilam said.\\n...\\n\\\"Hamas will anyway
refuse to completely disarm, and for now can continue to use Netanyahu as an excuse to avoid or at least slow down this process,\\\" he said.\\n...\\nNetanyahu had long campaigned on his close rapport
with Trump, who has taken unprecedented steps such as moving the US embassy to Jerusalem and joining Israel in attacking Iran.\\n...\\nBut Trump's popularity in Israel took a nosedive in April when he
called a ceasefire with Iran and sought a settlement, seeing the Middle East war as politically and economically damaging.\\n...\\nNetanyahu could be willing to take some steps forward on Gaza to
please Trump in return for new US action against Iran, Eilam said.\\n...\\n\\\"For Netanyahu, the Gaza Strip, and Lebanon too for that matter, are not the most urgent concerns; Iran is,\\\" he
said.\\n...\\n## - Tactical win for Hamas -\\n...\\nHamas publicly backed the disarmament agreement shortly after it chose a new leader, Khalil al-Hayya.\\n...\\n\\\"I think Hamas, from the get-go,
did this for tactical reasons,\\\" said Ghaith al-Omari, a former Palestinian Authority official who is now a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.\\n...\\nHe said that Hamas
wanted to be seen as a \\\"reasonable actor\\\" -- and that Netanyahu's rejection worked in its favour.\\n...\\n\\\"What this does is actually give Hamas and mediators reason to say, look, Hamas has
committed, Israel has not committed -- the ball is in Israel's court,\\\" he said.\\n...\\n\\\"It lets the pressure off Hamas.\\\"\\n...\\n## Trump to host Netanyahu\"], \"published_date\":

plan unlikely to be final word\\n\\n8 days ago\\n\\nShare\\n\\nSave\\n\\nAdd as preferred on Google\\n\\nYolande KnellMiddle East correspondent, Jerusalem\\n\\nEPA/Shutterstock\\n\\nBenjamin Netanyahu
is facing an uphill contest in a general election scheduled for Oct\", \"highlights\": [\"of Trump's 15-point Gaza plan unlikely to be final word\\n...\\nBenjamin Netanyahu is facing an uphill contest
in a general election scheduled for October\\n...\\nIsrael's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may have categorically rejected the new Board of Peace roadmap to disarm Hamas in Gaza, but that is
unlikely to be the final word.\\n...\\nThe White House is reportedly \\\"not bothered\\\" by Netanyahu's statement and views it as campaign rhetoric in the run-up to a heated general
election.\\n...\\nRecent days have seen an apparent pause in Israel's strikes on Gaza \\u2013 something Hamas had demanded when signing on to the US-backed, 15-point roadmap.\\n...\\nAnd there is
another suggestion that Israel is ready to advance US President Donald Trump's peace plan for Gaza\\u2013 getting ready for the deployment of the International Stabilization Force (ISF). The force is
made up of international troops, with the plan being for them to work with a new Palestinian police force to secure the territory.\\n...\\nIn July, after months of delicate negotiations, Trump
announced a \\\"major milestone\\\" in the implementation of his plan to end Israel's war in Gaza.\\n...\\nWriting on his Truth Social platform, Trump said that the Board of Peace had reached an
agreement for the complete disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups in the territory.\\n...\\nThe deal is meant to be carried out in phases, with all weapons decommissioned and stored
by a new Palestinian administration in Gaza \\u2013 which reports to the Board of Peace - and Israeli forces withdrawing from the more than 60% of Gaza they currently control.\\n...\\nSenior Hamas
officials confirmed that they had agreed to the new framework, conditioning it on mutual compliance by Israel. This was widely viewed as a major potential breakthrough in the conflict. The UK welcomed
it and the European Union hailed it as a \\\"crucial step\\\".\\n...\\nHowever, for more than a week, Israel did not give its formal response.\\n...\\nAn Israeli spokesman said only that the roadmap
did not \\\"reflect Israel's positions.\\\" A far-right member of the government, Itamar Ben-Gvir, wrote on X that the deal was \\\"unacceptable.\\\"\\n...\\nIncreasingly, mainstream Israeli
opposition politicians also raised doubts. They questioned whether all small arms would be decommissioned and the sequencing of the plan.\\n...\\nFinally on Sunday, Netanyahu told his cabinet, \\\"I
wish to be precise here: Israel does not accept the 15-point document.\\\"\\n...\\nHe added: \\\"The IDF [Israel Defense Forces] will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed. And when I
say the disarming of Hamas, it means heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry. And we are talking about genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament.\\\"\\n...\\nIn the same statement, the
prime minister described President Trump as \\\"the greatest of our friends in the White House\\\" but said that Israel knew \\\"how to stand firm\\\" against unacceptable ideas.\\n...\\nAny potential
concessions for Netanyahu would come at a politically sensitive moment.\\n...\\nHe is facing an uphill contest in the upcoming general election, scheduled for 27 October. It will be Israel's first
since the 7 October assault and three years on, Netanyahu has failed to secure what he vowed: \\\"absolute victory\\\" over Hamas.\\n...\\nThe former American diplomat and veteran Middle East
negotiator, Aaron David Miller, said the Israeli leader is facing \\\"the most consequential election\\\" of his political life.\\n...\\n\\\"He's navigating a very fine line between keeping his
constituents happy and not angering or alienating President Trump,\\\" he told the BBC.\\n...\\nFor now, he believes the White House recognises the situation and is giving Netanyahu \\\"a
pass.\\\"\\n...\\nMiller added: \\\"It's hard to believe that you're going to see any serious movement before you have another Israeli government.\\\"\\n...\\nIn the meantime, the Board of Peace has
been trying to reassure the Israeli public about the roadmap.\\n...\\nThe High Commissioner for Gaza, Nickolay Mladenov \\u2013 who led months of delicate negotiations with Hamas \\u2013 gave an
interview to Israel's Channel 12 just hours after Netanyahu's formal rejection of the roadmap.\\n...\\n\\\"Its goal is to make sure that Gaza is never again a threat to Israeli security and that what
happened before, [on] October 7, never happens again,\\\" he said.\\n...\\nHe said the deal takes \\\"a step-by-step approach\\\" meaning: \\\"If there is verified decommissioning of weapons, that
they are taken away from the factions and stored and ultimately rendered unusable, Israel then withdraws from Gaza.\\\"\\n...\\nUltimately, Mladenov said that nothing was being built \\\"on the basis
of trust\\\" but on \\\"verification.\\\"\\n...\\nHamas has since indicated that it still remains committed to the roadmap. It called on mediators and the Board of Peace to push for Israel to stick to
the terms agreed.\\n...\\nMeanwhile heavy pressure from Washington is likely to increase.\\n...\\nTrump is also looking at an important election this year \\u2013 November's midterm elections for the
US Congress. His Republican party faces the prospect of heavy losses, with petrol and grocery prices pushed up, in part due to Washington's unpopular five-month-long war in Iran.\\n...\\nThe US
president's own approval rating has tumbled, and he may well demand positive developments in his peace plan for Gaza in an effort to score a much-needed foreign policy win.\"], \"published_date\":

adopted on Nov. 17, 2025.\\n...\\nOn Aug. 3, four days after Trump\\u2019s announcement and three days after the BoP plan was released, Israeli officialdom broke its near-uniform
silence.\\n...\\nIsraeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich posted on X that \\u201cthe proposal published by the Board of Peace is not the plan presented to us in the [Security] Cabinet and not what

wrote.\\n...\\n\\u201cA blueprint that contradicts the war\\n...\\ncannot be promoted in Gaza. I will not allow such a plan to erase the\\n...\\n,\\u201d he added\\n...\\nThe same day, Israeli
President Isaac Herzog made clear that the position on disarmament was virtually uniform across the political spectrum, saying implementation of the BoP plan would depend on \\u201cthe clear caveat
and undertaking that Hamas must be disarmed.\\u201d\\n...\\nThe comments came hours before BoP chief Mladenov met in Jerusalem with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.\\n...\\nFollowing the
encounter, the BoP released a statement trumpeting that \\u201cIsrael and the Board of Peace share a common understanding of the ultimate objectives.\\n...\\n\\u201cThe goal is clear and is not in
question: the complete decommissioning of weapons in the Strip and the\\n...\\naway from rule by the gun to civilian governance,\\u201d it added. \\u201cContrary to inaccurate reports, we note that
the withdrawal of the IDF beyond the Yellow Line will take place only once decommissioning is complete, as Hamas committed to the mediators.\\n...\\napplies to light weapons, heavy weapons and the
tunnels alike.\\u201d\\n...\\nA senior source told JNS on Thursday that the Cabinet never voted on Trump\\u2019s original plan precisely because of widespread opposition to Palestinian
statehood.\\n...\\nNetanyahu \\u201caccepted the 20-point plan in his personal statement alongside President [Trump],\\u201d the senior source said. \\u201cThere is no official decision by the Israeli

several weeks ago granted the ISF immunity, paving the way for the force to begin operating. However, the government secretary clarified on Thursday that the formal agreement has not yet been
signed.\\n...\\nThe same senior officials told JNS that the U.S. administration is pressing for the deployment of the ISF as part of a broader move that would also include IDF withdrawals from
existing positions, and a cessation of targeted attacks on Hamas terrorists.\\n...\\n\\u201cCongratulations to Minister Smotrich, who withdrew his support for the introduction of the International
Stabilization Force for Gaza and joins me in firmly opposing this dangerous step,\\u201d Ben-Gvir told JNS.\\n...\\nLater on Sunday, Netanyahu closed the circle, leaving no doubt about where Israel
stands.\\n...\\n\\u201cIsrael rejects the [Board of Peace\\u2019s] 15-point document. The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed. And when I say Hamas must be disarmed, I mean
the heavy weapons, the less heavy weapons, all weapons. We are talking about genuine disarmament, not a fictitious one,\\u201d the prime minister said.\\n...\\n\\u201cContrary to all those who preach
to us, we do what needs to be done for Israel\\u2019s security, and we can and know how to stand our ground, even against our best friends when necessary.\\u201d\"], \"published_date\":

# Israeli Domestic Politics & the Board of Peace 15-Point Plan — Research Report
**Compiled 19 August 2026 | Horizon of interest: 10 September 2026 (22 days out)**

---

## 1. Headline finding that reframes the question

**Israel is not in a "coalition survival" situation — it is in a caretaker government mid-election-campaign.** The Knesset already dissolved itself in the early hours of **Friday 17 July 2026**, and the election is locked to **27 October 2026**. Smotrich and Ben Gvir therefore cannot "bring down" the government by bolting; there is no government left to bring down. The binding constraint has shifted from *parliamentary arithmetic* to *electoral competition for the same right-wing voters*, plus a set of **formal legal restraints on what a transitional government may decide**.

---

## 2. Election timing — settled, no ambiguity

| Fact | Date | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Coalition announces election date | 12 July 2026 | Haaretz, Israel Hayom, JC |
| Knesset votes to dissolve itself (Netanyahu votes in favour) | overnight 16–17 July 2026 | Haaretz |

| **Election day** | **27 October 2026** | Wikipedia, Al Jazeera, BBC |

- This was the **last possible date** — the 25th Knesset became the **first since 1988** to serve a full four-year term.
- On 10 September 2026, Israel will be **47 days from polling day**, in an active campaign.
- Likud held its primary on **17 August 2026** (results 18 August). Netanyahu launched his campaign with a Jerusalem mall walkabout on **Wednesday 12 August 2026** (Al-Monitor, 16 Aug).

## 3. Legal constraint: the Attorney-General's election-period restrictions

This is an under-covered but concrete obstacle to *formal* acceptance.

Following dissolution, **Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara** wrote to all ministers and to Government Secretary Yossi Fuchs:

- Election-period restrictions **now apply to the government**.
- Ministers must exercise **"considerable restraint"** in substantive decisions.
- Any decision **outside "routine government administration"** must first undergo **preliminary review by the ministry's legal adviser, in consultation with the AG's office**.
- Cited rationale: elevated risk that narrow partisan interests override the public interest, and concern that a caretaker government could **create "irreversible facts" limiting the next elected government**.
- She announced forthcoming detailed guidelines covering, explicitly, **"signing of international agreements."**
- The Government Secretariat was instructed that every proposed government or ministerial-committee decision must be accompanied by a legal opinion addressing these restrictions.

*(Israel National News #430328; Jerusalem Post #902948, published Friday after the overnight dissolution vote.)*

**Ben Gvir publicly dismissed the letter**, saying he never respected the AG's authority and vowing to seek her dismissal in the next Knesset term.

**Caveat I should flag:** this is advisory/procedural, not an absolute bar. A transitional Israeli government retains full legal powers. But it creates a formal procedural hurdle and an obvious litigation hook precisely for the category of act at issue — endorsing an international framework with irreversible territorial consequences.

## 7. Why formal acceptance is not a costless signature — the 24-hour trigger

This is the most important mechanical fact for anyone weighing "will Israel formally accept."

- **BBC (31 July 2026)**, having seen the annex: it requires Israeli forces to withdraw to the agreed **Yellow Line "within 24 hours of the Israeli government's approval of the plan,"** and not to return *"as long as Hamas complies with the implementation of the agreement."*
- **Roadmap point 2**: the timetable and implementation mechanisms for Phase 2 must be prepared **within 14 days after all parties approve** the roadmap.
- **Jerusalem Post (8 Aug 2026)**: cabinet ministers **broadly opposed** any step that could be read as entering the 14-day preparatory period, *because it would require restrictions on Israeli military operations, including targeted strikes.*

So formal approval starts an immediate operational clock — a withdrawal within 24 hours and a strike freeze — landing squarely in the campaign's final stretch. Israel currently controls **~60%** of Gaza (Netanyahu said in May 2026 the next step was 70%).

## 8. The substantive gaps that would have to be closed (JNS, 9 Aug 2026)

1. **Weapons fate** — Trump's point 13: destroy/remove all weapons, tunnels, infrastructure. BoP clause 8: NCAG will *"hold, store or control"* them.
2. **Sequencing** — BoP ties withdrawal to phased decommissioning administered by NCAG; Smotrich: it *"allows for an IDF withdrawal before the demilitarization is complete."*
3. **"Palestinian laws"** — appears in BoP points 6, 7, 9, 11; absent from Trump's plan. Minister Orit Strook called this the *"most antisemitic"* system since Nazi Germany.
4. **Statehood** — Trump point 19: one conditional future "pathway." BoP point 1: an explicit end goal (*"self-determination and Statehood"*).
5. **Terminology** — the word *"terrorism"* never appears in the BoP roadmap; it uses "militias"/"factions."
6. **Hamas personnel** — BoP point 7 lets vetted police who "fail" take *"alternative civilian roles"* while keeping *"financial rights."*
7. **Multinational force** — Smotrich: the roadmap *"changes the designation of the multinational force so that it will, in fact, limit IDF activity."*
8. **Reconstruction** — not conditioned on demilitarisation.

**Also relevant:** a senior source told JNS the Security Cabinet **never formally adopted Trump's original 20-point plan either** — Netanyahu endorsed it only in a *"personal statement"* alongside Trump, precisely because of internal opposition to the statehood clause. The established pattern is to approve narrow, technical, reversible components while withholding formal endorsement of the framework document.

**The trial:**
- Indicted November 2019 — Cases 1000, 2000, 4000 (bribery, fraud, breach of trust). Trial opened 2020.
- Netanyahu's own testimony ran from **December 2024** across **98 hearing days**; he stepped down from the stand after prosecutors concluded cross-examination.
- Trial resumed **15 July 2026** at Jerusalem District Court (Case 2000 testimony phase, including Minister **Ze'ev Elkin**), ran to **20 July**, then **summer recess**.
- **Proceedings resume in early September 2026** — i.e. essentially at the question horizon. Judges have decided hearings move to **five days a week** once the court returns from the October holidays.

**The pardon track:**
- **13 Oct 2025** — Trump urges Herzog to pardon Netanyahu, in the Knesset. **12 Nov 2025** — Trump follows up in writing on White House letterhead.
- **30 Nov 2025** — Netanyahu submits a **111-page pardon request**, without admitting guilt.
- **12 Feb & 5 Mar 2026** — Trump publicly attacks Herzog (*"should be ashamed"*; claims Herzog *"promised me five times"*). Herzog's office pushes back citing Israel's rule of law.
- **24 Mar 2026** — Heritage Minister **Amichai Eliyahu (Otzma Yehudit)** submits a 17-page recommendation to pardon (Justice Minister Levin having recused).
- **26 Apr 2026** — **Herzog defers the pardon decision**, calling for plea-deal mediation to be *"exhausted"* first; his office invites Netanyahu's lawyer and the AG to plea talks.

- **As of August 2026: no pardon, no plea deal, trial ongoing.**

**Implication:** Trump remains Netanyahu's most powerful advocate for clemency. This cuts *against* an outright humiliation of Trump — and is consistent with the observed "reject publicly, cooperate quietly" behaviour rather than with formal acceptance.

The dominant pattern in the evidence is what Al Jazeera's analysts and Al-Monitor both independently describe: **Netanyahu accepting operational components he can defend to the right, while withholding formal endorsement of the document itself.** Three public rejections (4, 5 and 9 August), a fourth restatement on 19 August via an Israeli official, and an outcome from the 17 August Kushner meeting consisting of two working groups with — per a senior Israeli official — no agreed composition, role, or timeline.

One search result (a Yahoo/JPost piece citing a "September 8" trial resumption) proved to be from 2025, not 2026, and I excluded it.*

## 💬 Response

I've submitted the structured findings. Summary of what the research established:

**The question's framing needs one correction:** there is no "coalition survival" problem, because there is no coalition left to collapse. The Knesset dissolved itself on 17 July 2026 and the election is locked to 27 October. Smotrich and Ben Gvir cannot bring the government down — what replaces that leverage is direct electoral competition for the same right-wing voters, plus formal legal restraints on what a caretaker government may decide.

**The strongest single piece of evidence** is Netanyahu's own reported words to Kushner on 17 August: progress on the 15-point framework is politically *"problematic"* ahead of 27 October. Reuters independently reports diplomats saying Israel is unlikely to make major concessions before the election, and the White House reportedly treats the rejections as campaign rhetoric.

**Three constraints I'd flag as under-appreciated:**

1. **The 24-hour trigger.** The roadmap annex requires withdrawal to the Yellow Line within 24 hours of government approval. Formal acceptance isn't a signing ceremony — it starts an immediate operational clock, which is why ministers specifically opposed even entering the 14-day preparatory period.
2. **The Attorney-General's election-period letter**, which requires legal pre-review of non-routine decisions and flags "signing of international agreements" for forthcoming guidelines. Procedural rather than absolute, but a real hurdle and a litigation hook.
3. **The precedent.** The Security Cabinet never formally adopted Trump's *original* 20-point plan either — Netanyahu endorsed it only in a personal statement, because of the statehood clause. The established pattern is approving narrow reversible components while withholding formal endorsement.

**Polling has severe house effects** — mainstream pollsters (Channel 12/13, Kan 11) put the Netanyahu bloc at 50–52; right-leaning ones (Channel 14, i24) at 58–63. The trend that matters: Otzma Yehudit rising 7→9→10 while Religious Zionism falls to 4, right at the threshold.

Two data-quality notes: AskNews returned 403 on this tier so all sourcing is web/Exa/direct fetch; and I discarded one search result citing a "September 8" trial resumption after checking it — that article is from 2025, not 2026. I found no external deadline tied to 10 September 2026; it appears to be the forecast horizon rather than a process milestone.
